meta.blurb: A wild moor, two haunted houses and a love too fierce for either. Heathcliff, a homeless boy, grows up beside Catherine Earnshaw, and when she chooses another man, his revenge reaches into the next generation. Emily Brontë's masterpiece, retold for learners.
meta.bible: Mr Lockwood: the new tenant of Thrushcross Grange, who visits Wuthering Heights in 1801 and hears the story. Heathcliff: a dark orphan brought from Liverpool by Mr Earnshaw; proud, silent, then bitter and revengeful; he dies at the end. Catherine Earnshaw: Mr Earnshaw's wild, high-spirited daughter, called Cathy; she marries Edgar Linton but loves Heathcliff; she dies after giving birth. Hindley Earnshaw: her older brother, jealous of Heathcliff, later a drunkard; he dies at the Heights. Mr Earnshaw: the kind old master of Wuthering Heights who brings Heathcliff home. Frances: Hindley's wife, who dies of illness after the birth of Hareton. Hareton Earnshaw: Hindley's son, raised rough and untaught by Heathcliff; he later learns to read. Edgar Linton: the gentle, rich master of Thrushcross Grange, who marries Catherine. Isabella Linton: Edgar's sister, who elopes with Heathcliff and later escapes. Linton Heathcliff: the weak, selfish son of Heathcliff and Isabella. Catherine Linton: also called Cathy, the daughter of Catherine and Edgar. Nelly Dean: the housekeeper who tells the story to Lockwood. Joseph: the old, harsh, religious servant at the Heights. Zillah: the housekeeper at Wuthering Heights. Wuthering Heights: the old farmhouse on the exposed moor, home of the Earnshaws. Thrushcross Grange: the elegant house in the valley, home of the Lintons. Yorkshire: the county in northern England. Liverpool: the port where Mr Earnshaw finds Heathcliff. Fixed facts: the story begins in 1801 and tells events over about thirty years; Heathcliff's ghost-like love for Catherine is the heart of it; Heathcliff is buried beside Catherine; Cathy and Hareton plan to marry on New Year's Day. Voice and tone: dark, passionate and stormy, told by Nelly with plain good sense; deaths are stated plainly with no gore; cruelty is shown without cruelty being praised.

A1A2: Mr Lockwood rented a quiet house and went to meet his landlord, Heathcliff.
The house was cold and dark, and the dogs jumped at him.
The next day it snowed, so Lockwood had to stay at the house.
Lockwood slept in an old bed and saw the name Catherine everywhere.
In a bad dream, a girl at the window asked to come in.
Lockwood was ill, so Nelly Dean sat with him and told a story.
Mr Earnshaw came home from Liverpool with a poor, dirty, hungry boy.
Hindley hated Heathcliff, but his sister Catherine liked the new boy.
Catherine and Heathcliff ran free on the moor every day.
Hindley went away to college, and then Mr Earnshaw died quietly.
Hindley came home with a wife and made Heathcliff a servant.
One night the two friends ran to look into the Grange.
A big dog bit Catherine, and the Lintons kept her there.
Catherine came home as a young lady, and Heathcliff felt small.
Hindley hit Heathcliff, and Heathcliff promised to pay him back.
Frances died after her son was born, and Hindley drank too much.
Edgar asked Catherine to marry him, and she said yes.
Catherine said that marrying Heathcliff would be a very bad thing.
Heathcliff ran away in a storm, and Catherine waited in the rain.
Edgar's parents caught her fever and died, and she married Edgar.
After three years, Heathcliff came back, and he was rich now.
Catherine was so happy to see him that Edgar felt afraid.
Heathcliff stayed at the Heights and played cards with Hindley.
Isabella Linton loved Heathcliff, but Catherine told her to stay away.
Edgar told Heathcliff to leave, and Catherine locked herself in her room.
Catherine was very ill and talked about when she was a child.
Heathcliff ran away with Isabella, and Edgar was very angry.
Isabella wrote to Nelly and said that her new life was terrible.
Heathcliff came to see Catherine, and they held each other and cried.
That night Catherine had a baby girl, and then she died.
Heathcliff cried out in pain and asked her ghost to stay.
Hindley drank until he died, and Heathcliff took his house.
Isabella ran away to London, and there she had a son.
Little Catherine grew up at the Grange, and her father loved her.
Cathy walked to Wuthering Heights and met her cousin Hareton.
Isabella died, and her son Linton came to live at the Grange.
Cathy and Linton wrote letters, but Nelly found them and burned them.
Heathcliff met Cathy on the moor and asked her to visit Linton.
Cathy visited Linton many times, though he was weak and selfish.
Heathcliff locked Cathy and Nelly in the house for several days.
They made Cathy marry Linton, and she cried the whole time.
Cathy ran home and was with her father when he died.
Soon after, Linton died, and Heathcliff owned both houses.
Cathy was lonely at the Heights, and she laughed at Hareton.
Cathy said sorry to Hareton and began to teach him to read.
Heathcliff no longer cared about revenge and stopped eating his food.
One morning they found Heathcliff dead, and the window was open.
They buried Heathcliff next to Catherine, as he had always wished.
Cathy and Hareton planned to marry on New Year's Day.
Lockwood looked at the three graves and thought that they slept in peace.
B1B2: Mr Lockwood has rented Thrushcross Grange, a quiet house in Yorkshire, and he walks across the moor to meet his landlord. The man's home, Wuthering Heights, stands alone on a hill where the wind never stops.
Heathcliff does not smile, and his old servant Joseph looks at the visitor with open dislike. When some fierce dogs attack Lockwood, nobody hurries to help him.
Lockwood returns the next day, but a heavy snowstorm begins and he cannot find his way home. Heathcliff refuses to lend him a guide, so he is forced to stay the night.

Zillah, the housekeeper, leads Lockwood to a room that nobody has used for years. The name Catherine is scratched all over the walls and window, and he finds an old diary written by a girl of that name.
That night Lockwood dreams that a cold child's hand grips his own at the window. “Let me in,” a voice cries, “I have been lost on the moor for twenty years.”
Lockwood walks home through the snow and falls seriously ill. While he rests, his housekeeper, Nelly Dean, begins to tell him the story of the people at the Heights.

Many years ago, old Mr Earnshaw walked to Liverpool and returned with a dirty, hungry child he had found in the street. He named the boy Heathcliff and told his family to treat him as one of their own.
Mr Earnshaw's son Hindley is jealous and often hits the newcomer. His daughter Catherine, a lively and wilful girl, soon becomes fond of the boy and refuses to leave his side.

The two children spend their days on the moors, running through the heather and escaping their lessons. Their favourite way to be punished is to be sent away together, and they laugh about it afterwards.
Hindley is sent away to college, and soon afterwards old Mr Earnshaw grows ill. He dies one evening in his chair by the fire, and the children are left without his protection.
Hindley returns for the funeral with a wife called Frances, and he is now the master of the house. He sends Heathcliff to work with the servants and forbids him to study.
One evening Catherine and Heathcliff run across the moor to Thrushcross Grange and look through a window. Inside, the rich Linton children, Edgar and Isabella, are crying over a little dog.
The Lintons' servants set a bulldog on the intruders, and it bites Catherine's ankle. Heathcliff is thrown out, but the Lintons take Catherine in and care for her for five weeks.
When Catherine comes home, she wears a fine dress and speaks like a young lady. Heathcliff, who is dirty from work, feels ashamed and wishes he were more like Edgar Linton.
When Edgar visits at Christmas, Heathcliff is humiliated in front of him, and Hindley beats him cruelly. Heathcliff swears that he will take revenge, even if it takes him years.
A year later Frances gives birth to a son called Hareton, but she is already ill and soon dies. Hindley is heartbroken, and he drinks and gambles until he becomes a danger to everyone around him.
Edgar Linton visits the Heights more often and finally asks Catherine to be his wife. She says yes at once, because he is rich, handsome and kind.
Catherine tells Nelly that it would lower her to marry Heathcliff, because he is so poor and so rough. She does not know that Heathcliff is sitting behind the settle and hears every word.
Heathcliff disappears, and that night a violent storm breaks over the moor. Catherine sits at the open window in the rain, calling for him, and she is soon seriously ill.
Mr and Mrs Linton catch Catherine's fever and die within a few days. A few months later, Catherine marries Edgar, and Nelly goes with her to live at Thrushcross Grange.
Three years later a tall, well-dressed man calls at the Grange, and Nelly hardly knows him. It is Heathcliff, who has come back with money, good manners and a hard, watchful look.
Catherine throws her arms around Heathcliff and laughs with joy. Edgar, however, watches them in silence, and he allows Heathcliff to visit only because he does not want to upset his wife.
Heathcliff goes to live at Wuthering Heights, where Hindley welcomes the chance to gamble with a rich man. Night after night Hindley loses, and Heathcliff slowly takes over all his debts.

Edgar's young sister Isabella falls in love with Heathcliff, who has been visiting the Grange often. Catherine warns her that he is cruel, like a wolf in the shape of a man, but Isabella does not listen.
Edgar finds Heathcliff kissing Isabella's hand and orders him to leave the Grange forever. Catherine is furious with her husband, and she locks herself in her bedroom and refuses to eat.
Catherine becomes delirious and tears feathers out of her pillow, talking of the moors where she played as a girl. When she opens the window, the cold air pours in, and Edgar rushes to her side.
While Catherine lies ill, Isabella slips away from the Grange and marries Heathcliff in secret. Edgar is deeply hurt, and he says that he will have nothing more to do with her.
Soon Isabella writes to Nelly that she has made a terrible mistake. Heathcliff is cruel to her and to everyone else, and she is afraid that he will do her real harm.
Heathcliff begs Nelly to let him see Catherine once more, and she lets him in while Edgar is at church. He takes the weak Catherine in his arms, and they weep and blame each other for their pain.
Edgar returns from church and finds the two of them together, and Catherine faints. That night she gives birth to a baby girl, and a few hours later she dies.
In the morning Nelly finds Heathcliff standing under a tree in the grey light, and he curses everything. He begs Catherine to haunt him, to drive him mad, as long as she never leaves him alone.
Six months later Hindley dies, drunk and almost without a penny. Because of his debts, Wuthering Heights now belongs to Heathcliff, who keeps young Hareton there and treats him like a servant.
Isabella escapes from her husband and goes to live near London, where she gives birth to a sickly son named Linton. She never goes back to Yorkshire, and Edgar does not see her again.
Edgar's daughter, also named Catherine, grows into a lively and warm-hearted girl. Edgar, who is still sad about his wife, protects her carefully and forbids her to go beyond the park wall.
When Cathy is thirteen, she walks past the garden wall and finds her way to Wuthering Heights. There she meets a rough young man named Hareton, who does not know that they are cousins.
When Isabella dies, Edgar travels south to fetch her thin, sickly son, who is twelve years old. Linton has barely arrived at the Grange when Heathcliff demands him and takes him away to the Heights.
Cathy has not forgotten her cousin, and the two of them begin to write to each other in secret. When Nelly finds out, she burns the letters and forbids Cathy to see him.
One day, while they are walking, Heathcliff meets Cathy and Nelly on the moor. He tells Cathy that her cousin is very ill and is longing to see her, and he invites them to the Heights.
Cathy sees how weak and spoiled Linton has become, but she pities him and promises to visit again. Before long she is secretly riding to the Heights every few days, and Nelly cannot stop her.

When Edgar becomes seriously ill, Heathcliff catches Cathy and Nelly on the moor and forces them into the Heights. He locks the door and tells Cathy that she will not go home until she has married Linton.
Cathy gives in at last, because she longs to see her dying father. She marries Linton, and Heathcliff will now own everything that Edgar's family has.
With Linton's help, Cathy escapes from the Heights and hurries home, arriving only just in time to say goodbye. Edgar dies peacefully a few hours later, with his daughter beside him.
Linton lives only a few weeks longer and dies young. Everything that belongs to Cathy now passes to Heathcliff, who owns both Wuthering Heights and Thrushcross Grange.
Cathy has to stay at the Heights, where she is bitter, lonely and rude to everyone. She laughs at Hareton because he cannot read well, and he turns away, hurt.
One day Hareton is hurt, and Cathy, ashamed of herself, offers to help him. After that she teaches him to read, and the two begin slowly to become friends.
Heathcliff watches the two young cousins and sees the dead Catherine in their faces. His revenge no longer interests him, and he grows silent, restless and distant, hardly eating anything for days.
One stormy night Heathcliff shuts himself in Catherine's old room with the window open. In the morning Nelly finds him lying dead on the bed, with a strange smile on his face.
Heathcliff is buried beside Catherine, exactly as he wished, and only a few villagers attend. Afterwards people say that they have seen the two of them walking together on the moor at night.

Cathy and Hareton fall in love, and they plan to marry on New Year's Day. They will leave Wuthering Heights and live together at Thrushcross Grange, while Joseph stays behind to guard the empty house.

Before he leaves Yorkshire, Lockwood walks to the churchyard and finds the three graves of Catherine, Edgar and Heathcliff. He listens to the soft wind in the grass and wonders how anyone could imagine restless sleep for the sleepers in that quiet earth.
C1C2: Seeking peace far from the noise of town, Mr Lockwood takes a tenancy at Thrushcross Grange and soon sets out across the moor to pay his respects to his landlord. The landlord's house, Wuthering Heights, crouches on an exposed hillside where the northern winds bend every tree away from the storm. Its owner, a dark and sullen man named Heathcliff, greets the visitor with a coldness that Lockwood mistakes for shyness.

Heathcliff offers his guest no smile and little conversation, while Joseph, the grim old servant, regards the stranger with undisguised contempt. When a pack of snarling dogs rushes at Lockwood, nobody in the household appears in any hurry to call them off. He leaves the house with his nerves badly shaken, yet his curiosity about its strange and joyless owner has, oddly enough, only been sharpened.

Undeterred by his reception, Lockwood returns the following day, only to be caught by a blinding snowstorm that makes the path across the moor impossible. Heathcliff, who will not spare a guide or a lantern, grudgingly allows him to remain until morning. Lockwood finds a strange household there: a rude young woman, a rough young man named Hareton, and no one willing to explain how they are related.

Zillah, the housekeeper, leads Lockwood quietly to a room that has stood unused for many years, and he settles into a large oak bed built like a closet. The name Catherine appears everywhere, scratched on the ledge and written in the margins of the dusty books, with the surnames Earnshaw, Heathcliff and Linton in turn. In the old diary of this girl he reads of bitter quarrels, of a cruel older brother, and of a boy she loved as a friend.

He sleeps badly, and in his dream a thin, icy hand reaches through the broken window and clutches his own with terrible strength. A small voice sobs that it has been wandering the moor for twenty years and begs him to let it in. His screams bring Heathcliff, who, believing himself alone, flings open the window and weeps, calling the name Catherine into the dark.

Lockwood struggles home through the drifts and soon falls into a fever that confines him to his bed for weeks. To pass the long hours, his housekeeper Nelly Dean, who has served both families for most of her life, offers to tell him what she knows of the people at the Heights. She begins her tale on a summer morning more than thirty years earlier, when the old master of Wuthering Heights set out on a long walk.

Nelly begins with old Mr Earnshaw, the master of Wuthering Heights, who left for Liverpool one morning and came back carrying a ragged, dark-haired orphan wrapped in his greatcoat. The child spoke a language no one could understand, so the master christened him Heathcliff, after a son who had died, and ordered his family to treat him as one of their own. From that day onward, the house at the Heights was never at peace again.

Hindley, the old man's son, resented the stranger for stealing his father's love and tormented him whenever the master looked away. Catherine, a wilful and high-spirited girl, took the opposite course and quickly attached herself to the silent boy, who never complained of his bruises. In time the two became inseparable, and every other relationship in the house grew pale beside theirs.

As the years passed, the two children spent every free hour roaming the moors, racing through the heather and escaping from the lessons and prayers that Joseph tried to force upon them. Punishment meant nothing to them so long as it was shared, and they treated every scolding as a joke. Together they built a private world, wilder and happier than any the house could offer.

Mr Earnshaw sent Hindley away to college, hoping that the boy's temper might improve with distance. Within a few years the old man himself began to fail, and one autumn evening he died quietly in his chair beside the fire. Heathcliff and Catherine, who had lost their only protector, sat on the stairs and wept together.

Hindley came home for the funeral accompanied by a nervous young wife named Frances, and he took charge of the Heights as its new master. Seizing the opportunity to repay old injuries, he stripped Heathcliff of his lessons and set him to work in the fields like a common labourer. Only Catherine still treated the boy as an equal, and he clung to her friendship with a quiet and dangerous loyalty.

One Sunday evening, escaping the gloom of the Heights, the two friends ran across the moor to Thrushcross Grange and crept up to a window glowing with candlelight. Inside they saw a warm and elegant room, where Edgar and Isabella Linton, pampered children of the house, were whimpering over a puppy. Heathcliff thought the sight a pitiful one and laughed at it, though Catherine, gazing at the warm light and the soft rugs, was not so sure.

The Lintons' bulldog seized Catherine by the ankle, and the servants dragged the two trespassers inside. Heathcliff was driven away as a ruffian, but Catherine was recognised, lifted into a chair and treated like a guest of honour. She remained at Thrushcross Grange for five weeks while her wound healed and her manners were polished.

When Catherine returned to the Heights, she stepped down from her horse in a silk dress and fine feathers, and she barely recognised the dirty boy who had waited for her. Heathcliff, looking at his own black hands, felt for the first time the full weight of his low position. He told Nelly that he wished he were fair and well dressed, like Edgar Linton.

When the Lintons came to visit at Christmas, Heathcliff was mocked in front of the guests, and Hindley, enraged by any sign of defiance, beat him without mercy. Lying in the dark, he told Nelly that he was planning a revenge so terrible that Hindley would never see it coming. He added, quite calmly, that he did not mind how long he had to wait.

In the summer Frances gave birth to a boy named Hareton, but she had long been weak with consumption and died only months after the christening. Hindley, mad with grief, abandoned all restraint and drowned his sorrow in drink and cards, growing more reckless with every passing month. The household learned to keep out of his way, and the servants stayed only through fear.

Edgar, who had fallen deeply in love with Catherine, called at the Heights with increasing frequency and eventually asked for her hand. She accepted at once, flattered by his wealth, his gentleness and the elegant life he promised her. Yet that night she confessed to Nelly that something inside her was uneasy, as though she had made a mistake that she could not name.

Catherine told Nelly that marrying Heathcliff would degrade her, since Hindley had reduced him to poverty and ignorance. Heathcliff, crouching unseen behind the high-backed settle, heard these words and crept out of the house without waiting to hear the rest. Had he stayed, he would have heard her say that she loved him more than herself and that she and he were the same.

Heathcliff vanished into the night, and soon a violent storm broke over the Heights, bringing down part of a chimney and flooding the lane. Catherine refused to leave the open window, soaked to the skin and calling his name into the darkness until she fell into a dangerous fever. The Lintons, hearing of her illness, kindly carried her to Thrushcross Grange, where she might be nursed back to health in comfort.

In nursing her, Mr and Mrs Linton caught the fever themselves, and within a few days both of them were dead. Catherine, recovering slowly and more subdued than before, soon consented to marry Edgar, and the wedding was held before the year was out. Nelly, who loved her young mistress, went with her to live at Thrushcross Grange.

Three years went by without a word, and then one warm evening a tall and well-dressed stranger appeared at the door of the Grange. It was Heathcliff, now wealthy and manly, with a polished manner and a hard, watchful look that gave nothing away of how he had made his fortune. Nelly, who had known him as a ragged boy, recognised him only when he spoke her name in the voice she remembered.

Catherine ran to him and laughed and wept by turns, so overjoyed that she scarcely noticed her husband's pale and silent face. Edgar tolerated the visit rather than risk her anger, but he disliked and distrusted the newcomer from the beginning. Nelly, watching them both with growing dread, felt in her heart that nothing but trouble would come of Heathcliff's return to the neighbourhood.

Heathcliff lodged at the Heights, paying Hindley handsomely for the privilege, and the two men spent their evenings gambling and drinking. Hindley, who was already deep in debt, lost more each night, while his lodger quietly gathered up his promissory notes and mortgages. Piece by piece, the house that had once rejected the orphan was passing into his hands.

Edgar's sister Isabella, a sheltered girl of eighteen, fell passionately in love with the dark, mysterious visitor. Catherine, who understood him far better than anyone, warned her that he was savage and merciless, a wolf in the shape of a man, and begged her to think no more of him. Isabella heard only what she wished to hear, and Heathcliff, noticing her devotion, began to see a use for it.

When Edgar discovered that Heathcliff was courting his sister, he ordered the intruder out of the house, and a bitter quarrel followed between the husband and wife. Catherine, torn between the two men she loved, locked herself in her room, refused all food and declared that she would starve rather than yield. Three days later, after hours of silence and refusal, she was no longer able to tell the difference between the room and her dreams.

In her fever Catherine tore her pillow to pieces, scattering the feathers and murmuring about the moors where she had played as a child. She flung open the window to feel the wind of the heights upon her face, and when Edgar came to hold her back she did not seem to know him. For the first time since her marriage, the doctor spoke gravely of danger, and the whole house waited in anxious silence.

While Catherine lay ill, Isabella slipped out of the house one night and eloped with Heathcliff, who wanted her family's fortune as much as he wanted revenge on Edgar. Her brother, deeply wounded by the betrayal, announced that he would have no further dealings with her and would offer her no help. Nelly saw that the web Heathcliff had been spinning had become much larger than she thought.

A few weeks later a letter came from Isabella, in which she begged for news of her brother and confessed that she had married a man she could not describe as human. Heathcliff, she wrote, treated her with open contempt and relished every unhappy hour she spent in that house. She wondered, with a bitterness that seemed to scorch the paper, how any woman could ever have loved him or hoped to change him.

Heathcliff begged Nelly, with a desperation she had never before seen in him, to arrange a last meeting, and against her better judgement she waited until Edgar left for church and let the visitor in. He gathered the frail woman into his arms, and she told him that he had broken her heart, while he answered that she had broken her own by choosing Edgar and wealth. Even so, neither would let go of the other, as though they might somehow stay together by refusing to part.

Edgar returned from church earlier than expected, and as he hurried into the room, Catherine fell insensible into the arms of her husband. She never recovered her senses, but at midnight she gave birth to a daughter, and a few hours later, in the quiet before dawn, she passed away. Edgar sat by her bed, broken with grief, and did not move for hours.

At dawn Nelly found Heathcliff beneath an old tree in the garden, his face grey and his eyes wild, howling like a wounded animal. He prayed that Catherine might never rest, that she might haunt him all his days, drive him mad if she must, as long as she never left him alone. Nelly felt a strange and unwilling pity for the man who had caused so much sorrow.

Within months of Catherine's funeral, Hindley drank himself to death, leaving only debts and a ruined estate. Heathcliff, who held every mortgage, now owned Wuthering Heights outright and took Hindley's son Hareton as his own, treating the boy exactly as Hindley had once treated him. He allowed Hareton to grow up rough and uneducated, in the hope that the child would never rise above his station.

Having endured a few months of Heathcliff's cruelty, Isabella fled in the night and settled in the south of England, where she later gave birth to a frail and fretful boy. She named him Linton and kept him far from the moors, never again setting foot in the county where she had suffered so much. Her brother Edgar, who could not forgive her, would not so much as write.

The little daughter, who was also named Catherine, grew into a bright and warm-hearted child with her mother's dark eyes and her father's gentle nature. Edgar, haunted by his loss, devoted himself entirely to her upbringing and forbade her to walk beyond the garden wall, never mentioning that a second house stood on the hill. She obeyed her father in all things, but she never quite stopped wondering what lay beyond the hills she could see from her window.

At thirteen, while Nelly's back was turned, Cathy slipped away and walked for miles across the moor until she reached the strange grey house on the hill. There she met Hareton, a strong and untaught young man who showed her the way back, though neither of them yet knew they were cousins. Nelly, who found her at last, was begged by the frightened girl to keep the whole story from her father.

When Isabella fell ill and died, Edgar went himself to bring her son home to the Grange, and Cathy waited eagerly for a new companion. But Linton, a pale and peevish boy of twelve, had no sooner arrived than Heathcliff demanded him, and Edgar, who had no legal right to refuse, gave him up. The boy was taken to the Heights the very next day, and Cathy, crying in her room, did not see him go.

Cathy, who had thought of Linton ever since the day he left, began a secret correspondence with him that grew warmer with every letter. Nelly, discovering a hidden bundle of notes, burned them in the kitchen fire and warned her young mistress that nothing good could come of a friendship with Heathcliff's son. Cathy cried and begged and promised to obey, but in her stubborn young heart she was not truly convinced of anything.

While walking on the moor one afternoon, Cathy and Nelly were stopped by Heathcliff, who told them with surprising gentleness that Linton was wasting away for love of his cousin. He urged Cathy to visit the sick boy, and she, who had never imagined that this stranger might be a cruel man, agreed at once. Nelly, who trusted none of this, followed unwillingly and with a growing unease into the house at the Heights.

Cathy found her cousin pale and fretful, and to her young mind his weakness seemed a call for kindness rather than a defect of character. She returned again and again, convincing herself that she could lift his spirits, while Linton, selfish and easily frightened, grew accustomed to taking everything she offered. Heathcliff, who had arranged every step of this meeting, watched the affection ripen like fruit in the sun and smiled.

With Edgar sinking fast, Heathcliff intercepted the two women on the moor and herded them into the Heights, then locked the doors and pocketed the key. He told Cathy, in a voice of quiet menace, that she would remain a prisoner until she had agreed to marry his son. Nelly, shut in another room, could only wait and listen to the girl's furious protests.

After a day of threats and tears, Cathy at last gave way, for she longed above all else to see her father once more before he died. She was married to Linton, who showed little interest in the ceremony, and by this act, Heathcliff secured the right to claim everything that would one day have been hers. Even then, with the vows spoken and the weeping girl standing before him, he showed no intention of letting her go.

Helped at last by the frightened Linton, Cathy escaped from the Heights and ran home to find her father still living, though only just. Edgar recognised his daughter, spoke a few quiet words, and died peacefully that night, murmuring that he was going to join his Catherine. After the funeral, Heathcliff arrived at the Grange without ceremony and took Cathy back to the Heights as his daughter-in-law.

Linton, who had never been strong, faded and died within weeks, and under the law everything that Cathy owned passed into Heathcliff's hands. At last he held both Wuthering Heights and Thrushcross Grange, and every person he had once hated was either dead or in his power. He then rented the Grange to strangers, among them, in time, a quiet gentleman named Lockwood, who knew nothing of its past.

Cathy, now a widow at seventeen, lived on at the Heights, miserable and often rude, with no friend in the house but a servant who pitied her. She scorned Hareton for his ignorance and laughed at him whenever he tried to read aloud, until he gave up and threw his books into the fire. Beneath all his roughness and silence, he had admired her from the day they first met and was hurt more deeply than he showed.

When Hareton was hurt in an accident, Cathy at last felt ashamed of her cruelty, and she offered him a book as a peace-making gift. Little by little she taught him to read, and as his reading improved, his manner softened, and he began to take pains over his appearance. The quarrelling cousins gradually learned to talk, to laugh and to depend upon one another.

As the cousins grew closer, Heathcliff found that he had lost his appetite for revenge, since every time he looked at Hareton or Cathy he saw only the face of the woman he had lost. He wandered the house at night, refused to eat and spoke of the nearness of the end, with an odd, bright look in his eyes. All his careful plans for ruin now seemed as worthless to him as ashes, and he could no longer remember why he had made them.

One stormy night Heathcliff locked himself in the old oak-panelled room that had once been Catherine's, and in the morning Nelly found the window swinging in the rain. He lay on the bed, with his eyes open and a fierce, joyful look on his face, quite dead. Nelly, in her horror and bewilderment, could not bring herself to close his eyes.

Heathcliff was buried beside Catherine at the edge of the churchyard, under the open sky, as he had once commanded. Only Hareton wept at the grave, and before long the neighbours began to whisper that Heathcliff and his Catherine had been seen walking together on the moor on wild nights. Old Joseph, who believed every word of such tales, declared with grim satisfaction that the devil himself had come to carry off the master.

Hareton, who had grown into a thoughtful and gentle man, and Cathy, who had lost her pride and her bitterness, were soon deeply in love, and they arranged to be married on New Year's Day. They would leave Wuthering Heights to Joseph and the ghosts, and move to the comfort of the Grange. Nelly rejoiced in the plan from the bottom of her heart, believing that two broken families had finally begun to heal.

On his last evening in Yorkshire, Lockwood walked to the churchyard and found the three headstones standing side by side at the edge of the moor, Catherine's grey and weathered, Edgar's half covered with moss, and Heathcliff's still bare. He lingered among the heather and the harebells, watching the moths flutter above the grass and listening to the soft wind. He wondered, as he turned away, how anyone could imagine restless sleep for the sleepers in that quiet earth.
